subject: anatomy
title: Cranial nerves: nuclei, exit foramina and clinical lesions

steps.tx: Twelve pairs of **cranial nerves** originate from the forebrain and brainstem to innervate the head, neck and visceral organs. Cranial nerves one and two arise from the cerebrum and diencephalon. Cranial nerves three and four emerge from the midbrain. Cranial nerves five through eight emerge from the pons and pontomedullary junction. Cranial nerves nine through twelve arise from the medulla oblongata, exiting via basal skull foramina.

steps.tx: The **facial nerve** possesses complex motor, parasympathetic, sensory and taste functions. Motor fibres from the motor nucleus loop around the abducens nucleus, forming the facial colliculus, before exiting at the cerebellopontine angle. It travels through the internal acoustic meatus, facial canal and stylomastoid foramen. Branches include the greater petrosal nerve for lacrimation, nerve to stapedius for sound dampening, and chorda tympani for taste and salivation.

vis.alt: Course of the facial nerve: internal acoustic meatus, geniculate ganglion giving greater petrosal nerve, facial canal giving nerve to stapedius and chorda tympani, stylomastoid foramen giving posterior auricular and digastric branches, then the parotid plexus with five terminal branches.
vis.caption: Branches come off in order of the nerve's route; the parotid plexus gives temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.

steps.tx: The distinction between upper and lower motor neuron **facial palsy** is clinically vital. Upper motor neuron lesions from contralateral cerebral hemisphere stroke spare forehead wrinkling because the frontalis muscle receives bilateral corticonuclear innervation. Lower motor neuron lesions such as Bell palsy or acoustic neuroma affect all ipsilateral facial muscles, resulting in loss of forehead wrinkling, incomplete eye closure and drooping mouth angle.
steps.say: The distinction between upper and lower motor neuron facial palsy is clinically vital. Upper motor neuron lesions from contralateral stroke spare forehead wrinkling because the frontalis muscle receives bilateral innervation. Lower motor neuron lesions such as Bell palsy affect all ipsilateral facial muscles, causing loss of forehead wrinkles, incomplete eye closure and mouth drooping.

left.title: Upper motor neuron lesion
points: Lower facial weakness on opposite side

right.title: Lower motor neuron lesion
points: Forehead wrinkling lost on same side
Inability to close eye on same side
May lose taste and exhibit hyperacusis

steps.tx: The **jugular foramen** transmits cranial nerves nine, ten and eleven along with the internal jugular vein. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and sensation from the posterior tongue and carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents. The vagus nerve supplies parasympathetic fibres to thoracic and abdominal viscera. The accessory nerve innervates sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Jugular foramen syndrome manifests with hoarseness, dysphagia and shoulder drop.
